The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

The question

What does an Apezone photograph look like — and what is off-limits? Not the logo, not the type. Photography, texture, release artwork, and whether the ornate 2015 artwork carries forward.

The answer, in one paragraph

Photograph the band the way you would photograph five people who have been doing this for thirty years and are not trying to impress you: available light, nobody lit, nobody retouched. The finished pictures are black and white, cold in the shadows, and they run all the way from true black to true white — on a dark page the photograph is the thing that carries the light. The 2015 ornament is retired — it belongs to that record, not to the band.

One practical thing came out of this that nobody expected, and it changes how a gig gets booked. It is in The thing to ask a venue below.

This was rebuilt on 2 August after Marcus reviewed the first version and said the photographs came out too dark against an already-dark palette, and asked why a professional photographer’s work was being re-processed at all. Both objections were right and both were measurable. What changed is in sections 02 and 03.

01

The band already knew the answer

The plan argued that the photography should be documentary and unglamorous rather than posed and lit. An argument is not evidence, so it got tested against the band’s own archive — and the archive agrees, twice, thirteen years apart, without anyone having decided it.

One correction to the plan

The plan said documentary rather than posed and lit, treating those as one thing. They are not. The best frame above is posed — four people were asked to stand in a line and did. What is banned is lighting and retouching, not arranging people. So the rule is narrower and more useful: arrange the people; do not light them, and do not fix them afterwards.

02

What was wrong, and what it is now

The correction

The first version converted every photograph onto the brand’s colour ramp and capped how bright it was allowed to get, reasoning that a photograph brighter than the text beside it pulls the eye to the wrong place. That reasoning is wrong in practice, and the measurements were not close: every picture ended up with the same brightest point, average brightness dropped about 40%, and one frame ended up with less contrast against the page than a button is required to have.

Marcus described it as dark on dark eating the band’s energy. That is exactly what the numbers say. On a dark page the photograph is the thing that carries the light — so the cap is gone, and photographs now run from true black to true white.

The narrower concern underneath the mistake is real, and it survives as a layout rule instead: where words sit on top of a photograph, darken a panel behind the words. Do not dim the whole picture to protect a caption.

A colour version was tested, and not chosen

The second half of the objection was that black and white costs the band its spark. So an alternative was built that keeps colour, but only the brand’s own two colours — a red stage light comes out as the warm gold from the palette rather than being stripped. It works: a frame measuring 57.6% red comes out at 0.00% and still looks warm.

Marcus chose black and white anyway — “monochrome is better than the one with the yellowish tint”. It is recorded here rather than dropped, because it worked and might suit a particular record later. Two marks against it: it changes what the room actually looked like, and it needs the original camera files to have anything to work with.

Include the boring frames. Hands, cases, cables, an empty room. A set that is all faces reads as a promo shoot; the unremarkable frames are what makes it read as a record of an evening.

03

When not to process anything at all

The other half of the question: why process photographs a professional has already finished? The answer is that you should not, and the first version did.

So the rule is

The treatment is a specification, and a photographer is given the numbers and works to them. They will do it better than a script, because they were in the room. The software exists for two narrower jobs: checking whether a delivered picture already meets the specification, and rescuing material that never had a grade — phone frames, old scans, anything the band shoots itself.

The check is worth having because it is not always obvious by eye. It measures whether a photograph reaches true black and true white, whether it is genuinely colourless, whether any red survives, whether there is enough detail to work with at all — and, since this is what went wrong, whether the picture is bright enough to lift off the page it sits on.

04

The thing to ask a venue

This is the most useful thing the task produced, and it was not in the brief.

A photograph taken under strong coloured stage lighting cannot be rescued. Not by this recipe, not by any other. Once the colour is removed there is nothing underneath — the person is a flat silhouette in front of a blown-out lamp, and everything in between is smoke.

It is measurable, which means it can be checked before anyone wastes time

The obvious measurement does not catch this — a black silhouette against a white lamp has plenty of contrast on paper. What is missing is detail in the middle tones, and that can be measured directly. Frames that work score 0.093–0.130. Frames lost to coloured lighting score 0.019–0.061. Nothing tested lands in the gap between.

So a whole shoot can be checked in seconds and the unusable frames dropped before anyone starts choosing favourites.

Ask when the gig is booked White or near-white front lighting, at least for the first three songs. Said on the night, it is too late.
Much of the 2011 live archive is unusable The Palojoki and Rautaruukki folders are almost all coloured wash. Worth knowing before a campaign is planned around old photographs.
Nummela 2012 is the exception White stage light, full resolution, and it processes cleanly. The best live photography the band has — with one condition, below.
05

Grain

The logo is flat and clean. The photographs should not be — a band whose pictures are as crisp as its logo looks like a software company. So the photographs carry a small amount of film-like grain. The risk is obvious: grain is also the fastest route straight back to the 2011 look, so it gets a fixed amount rather than a judgement call.

One exception, and it needs a reason

A single practical light that was really in the room — a bulb, an amplifier light, an exit sign — may be kept warm. Could you point at the lamp? If yes, keep it. If the warmth is the air rather than a lamp, the picture goes cold. Given the choice above, that is an exception rather than a style.

06

How a record sleeve is built

Which one depends on the record. A photograph when there is something real to photograph; a sign when the record has a joke or an idea in it; type alone when there is nothing honest to show — which, for an album finished in 2013 and never released, is the truthful answer.

The middle one is coming back — subject to the founders

It comes from the band’s own first record: Unbalanced, 1999, wore a yellow warning triangle with a figure slipping over, punning on the title. Round C rebuilt that as one sign per release — falling rocks for Get Stoned With Alexis, a sun over a horizon for Tomorrow Is A New Day.

Marcus agreed to it on 3 August, and said in the same breath that it has to go to Manu as well, because the 1999 joke is from before his time in the band. So it is provisionally adopted: design work can proceed on that basis, and nothing goes out under it until Manu, Jukka and Tuomas have seen it.

Worth being clear about what is being agreed to. It is not a style — it is a promise that every future record will have a one-line idea that can be drawn as a road sign. That is a decision about the records, not the artwork.

One rule comes with it: signs are drawn from real signage only. A falling figure and falling rocks stay deadpan. A banana skin or a cartoon monkey ends the whole system in one release.

07

The 2015 artwork does not continue

This is the best-made work in the whole archive and its colour was measurably the most disciplined the band has ever had — that discipline is exactly what the new palette inherited. So the discipline continues. The drawing does not.

The reason is simple: that artwork is about Aleksis Kivi. The ornamental style belongs to his century, the cabin is the world of those songs, the lettering is a nineteenth-century title page. Every part of it points at the record’s subject, which is why it works so well — and why it cannot be the band’s permanent identity. Marcus made this point himself: it was a costume for one record. Keeping it would mean quoting an eleven-year-old release every time the band says its own name.

Still fine A reissue of the 2015 EP keeps its own sleeve. A post about 2015 shows the 2015 artwork. That is the record being shown, not the band being dressed.
Off-limits New ornament drawn in 2027 — new scrollwork, new blackletter, new floral frames. There is no version of that which is not the band imitating its own past.
08

Off-limits

The most useful part of the document, and the part meant to be read before starting anything. Four of the failure modes are shown rather than described, because they are all cheap to produce by accident and much easier to recognise than to remember.

Not thisWhy
Red, anywhereIncluding as a tint, a filter, or one red object left red. Decided on measurement in the colour work, not on taste. In a photograph — the stills are monochrome, so it cannot survive the conversion anyway. Colour footage is scoped (2026-08-04): a red cable in a rehearsal room is the room; what is forbidden is red the production chooses, and graphics laid over the footage stay absolute.
RetouchingNo smoothing, no whitened teeth, no sharpening, no replaced skies. Thirty years is the asset; making four men look younger throws it away.
Added textureNo paper overlays, dust and scratches, light leaks, torn edges or lens flare. Grain is the only texture in a photograph.
Stars near the skullTwo thirds of the 2011 badge. Nobody would do this deliberately; it is on the list because it happens by accident.
Menace announcedBlood, barbed wire, fog machines, chains, snarling. The identity implies; it does not announce.
Visual jokesNo monkey comedy, no banana, no gorilla suit, nothing that winks. Settled by Marcus: the identity stays straight so that the jokes in the records and the writing land harder.
Invented captionsNo made-up dates, archive references, Latin names or institutions. Not on artwork, and not on photograph credits either.
Naming who is in a photographNot unless someone who was there has confirmed it. See the limits below.
AI photographs of the bandFive real, identifiable people. This needs a camera and an afternoon.
The test that catches what a list cannot

Would a joke survive being placed in this frame? If a dry caption or a daft sleeve would look like a mistake against the photography, the art direction has gone too solemn. The water bottle in the third picture at the top of this page is the calibration: an unposed, faintly ridiculous detail inside an otherwise straight photograph. Keep frames that can hold one of those.

09

Limits, and what still needs the band

Confirm the sign programme with Manu, Jukka and Tuomas

Marcus has agreed to it. The Unbalanced joke is from 1999, so the three who made it should see it before anything ships under it. One image to show them: c1-hazard/system-sheet-night.png.

Which Nummela 2012 photographs are Apezone?

Marcus confirmed that Apezone played Nummela in November 2012 as the warm-up band for Honey Hellraiser — which is why the other band’s backdrop is on stage in most of the frames. It also means the shoot covers a whole evening and two bands, across 197 photographs.

This is the best live photography the band has, and none of it can be published as a picture of Apezone until someone who was there says which frames are which. It is worth an hour of somebody’s time. The gig itself was not recorded anywhere and has now been added to the band history.

Who is in the backstage photograph?

The graffitied-room frame appears three times in this report, always for its light rather than as a picture of the band, because who is in it has never been established. Same rule as above before it goes anywhere public.

  • No photograph here was taken for this brand. Every frame is old material being used to work out a treatment. The treatment has never been applied to a photograph shot with it in mind, and the first real shoot may well find something this got wrong.
  • Nothing has been printed. Everything is specified for screens. A photograph on uncoated paper will not look like it does here; print one before committing to a press kit.
  • Some photographs cannot carry a page whatever is done to them. The backstage frame stays too dark even after a lift, because it is a genuinely dark room. The answer there is not to run it full width.
  • The first version of this was wrong and it shipped. It was built and committed before anybody looked at a photograph inside a layout — only on comparison sheets, where a flat treatment reads as restraint. Marcus caught it on the page. Worth recording, because it will apply again: a treatment for a dark identity has to be judged on the dark surface.
  • Nothing on this page was generated. Every photograph comes from the band’s own archive. The image-generation budget for this task was six; none of it was used.
  • Video is not covered, and it was named as a place the humour lives. That is a gap for later, not a problem now.

A few terms

Grade
The processing applied to a photograph to give it a consistent look — brightness, contrast and colour. Here it is a piece of software rather than somebody’s eye, so it gives the same answer every time.
Grain
The fine speckled texture of photographic film. Digital photographs do not have it, so a small amount is added.
Palette
The fixed set of colours the brand is allowed to use. Here that is a near-black, a slate grey, an off-white, and one warm gold.
Documentary
Photographs that record what was actually there, rather than a scene built for the camera.
Stage wash
Coloured light thrown across a whole stage, as opposed to white light pointed at the people on it.
Sleeve
The cover artwork of a record.
